newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish minister denies third charge in four days.
newsitem.headline: Spanish minister denies third charge in four days.

text.p: Spain's embattled Defence Minister Eduardo Serra wearily denied on Thursday the third graft charge against him in four days, saying the stream of press accusations was beginning to take its toll.

"I don't think anything can be found where I consciously did something unlawful," Serra told a radio interviewer. "The problem is that "keep slandering, something will eventually stick' is beginning to hurt."

The latest charge is that when Serra, an independent politician, was secretary of state for defence under the previous Socialist administration he awarded in 1982 a multi-million-dollar contract for a nuclear bunker to a company at which he became vice-president six years later.

Like the previous two accusations this week it was published by the daily El Mundo, whose investigative reporting played a major role in revealing a series of scandals that brought to an end 13 years of Socialist rule.
Conservative Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar gave his full backing on Wednesday to Serra, who according to Spanish media owes his job to King Juan Carlos.
"Old times will not come back. The days of corruption scandals will not return," Aznar told reporters.

He dismissed calls by his Basque allies for the resignation of his minister, who had acknowledged the day before making hundreds of calls recommending friends for public contracts and other favours but denied the previous two corruption charges.
Aznar took office four months ago on a clean-hands platform after lambasting the Socialists for countless scandals, many of them revealed by El Mundo.

The daily on Monday quoted court documents as showing Serra had already been promoted from vice-president to chief executive of major construction company Cubiertas when it paid more than $1 million in bribes in return for contracts from then-Civil Guard chief Luis Roldan.
On Tuesday, the daily said Serra had interceded on behalf of a brother-in-law in 1986 for a contract from the paramilitary Civil Guard.
"Frankly, I don't know if I ever made such a request in a telephone call," the minister said on the day that charge was published. "It's possible."
He added: "As you know, one makes hundreds of calls on behalf of someone else... Even if it was true, it would only be a run-of-the-mill recommendation like the ones you do by the hundreds."

Serra has few friends in Aznar's Popular Party (PP). He has been in the spotlight for weeks over a reported tug-of-war with Deputy Prime Minister Francisco Alvarez Cascos about control of Spain's intelligence services.
He was also criticised as one of the key movers in a surprise government decision to turn down court requests to declassify files on the 1980s "dirty war" on Basque ETA rebels.
The 1983-87 campaign of bombings, kidnappings, torture and murder killed 27 people, one-third of them by mistake.
